title: Peripheral Artery Disease: Limb Risk and Vascular Risk Together
bottomLine: PAD is both a limb disease and a systemic ASCVD marker. Confirm the diagnosis with vascular examination and ABI/appropriate imaging, distinguish claudication from acute or chronic limb-threatening ischemia, then combine exercise/smoking treatment, antithrombotic and lipid-risk reduction with timely vascular referral when limb viability is threatened.
recognize: Exertional calf/thigh/buttock discomfort relieved by rest, diminished pulses, bruits and trophic changes support PAD.
Rest pain, nonhealing ulcers or gangrene suggest chronic limb-threatening ischemia; sudden pain/pallor/pulselessness/paresthesia/paralysis suggests acute limb ischemia.
differentiate: Neurogenic claudication and musculoskeletal pain have different triggers/relief patterns.
Diabetes/CKD can cause noncompressible arteries and misleading ABI values, requiring alternative vascular testing.
assessment: Assess pulses, skin/ulcers, neurologic function, walking limitation, smoking, diabetes, CKD, CAD/cerebrovascular disease and foot-care capacity.
workup: Use ABI as a first-line physiologic test when interpretable, with toe pressures/duplex/vascular imaging when ABI is nondiagnostic or revascularization planning is needed.
management: Use smoking cessation, structured exercise, intensive lipid/BP/diabetes management and antiplatelet/vascular therapy according to current CCS PAD guidance.
Urgently refer acute limb ischemia and promptly refer chronic limb-threatening ischemia or lifestyle-limiting disease despite therapy.
medicationSafety: Antithrombotic intensification increases bleeding risk and should follow indication-specific PAD/ASCVD guidance.
Avoid compression or routine wound strategies that ignore severe arterial insufficiency.
counselling: Teach foot inspection, smoking cessation and that PAD signals elevated heart/stroke risk even when leg symptoms are mild.
followUp: Track walking function, wounds and cardiovascular risk targets; ensure vascular referrals and imaging are closed-loop.
examTrap: Treating PAD as only a leg-pain problem and missing its systemic ASCVD risk—or delaying acute limb ischemia for outpatient ABI testing.
oneLinePearl: PAD threatens both the limb and the cardiovascular future.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society 2022 Peripheral Arterial Disease Guideline

title: DVT and PE: Confirm VTE, Classify Risk, Anticoagulate Safely
bottomLine: VTE care has three steps: use pretest probability to confirm or exclude thrombosis, identify high-risk PE or threatened limb, then choose anticoagulation and treatment duration based on provoking factors, cancer/pregnancy/renal function, bleeding risk and recurrence risk.
recognize: Unilateral swelling/pain can indicate DVT; dyspnea, pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, tachycardia, syncope or hemoptysis can indicate PE.
differentiate: D-dimer rules out selected low/intermediate-probability disease; it does not diagnose VTE.
Cellulitis, Baker cyst, heart failure and musculoskeletal disease can mimic DVT; pneumonia/ACS/pneumothorax can mimic PE.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, bleeding risk, provoking factors, prior VTE, cancer, pregnancy, renal/hepatic function and antithrombotic interactions.
workup: Use validated probability pathways with compression ultrasound or appropriate PE imaging.
Assess RV strain/biomarkers when PE risk stratification will change treatment/disposition.
management: Start anticoagulation when indicated and safe; unstable/high-risk PE requires emergency reperfusion evaluation.
Set treatment duration according to transient vs persistent provoking factors and recurrence/bleeding balance; selected low-risk PE can be outpatient only with reliable support/follow-up.
medicationSafety: DOAC, LMWH and warfarin selection differs with pregnancy, renal function, cancer, interactions and bleeding risk.
Routine INR does not measure DOAC anticoagulant effect.
counselling: Teach adherence, bleeding precautions, interaction review and emergency symptoms of PE/major bleeding.
followUp: Review duration, recurrence risk, bleeding and persistent dyspnea/post-thrombotic symptoms.
examTrap: Calling a positive D-dimer VTE or continuing anticoagulation indefinitely without revisiting why the event occurred.
oneLinePearl: Probability diagnoses VTE; provoking factors and bleeding risk shape how long you treat it.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada DVT/PE and duration-of-treatment clinical guides

title: Syncope: Identify the Dangerous Cause Before Calling It Vasovagal
bottomLine: Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion. History, orthostatic vitals when appropriate and ECG drive the first pass; exertional events, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, family sudden death, major bleeding or persistent neurologic/cardiopulmonary symptoms make discharge unsafe.
recognize: Vasovagal syncope often has trigger/prodrome and rapid recovery; cardiac syncope may be abrupt, exertional or associated with structural disease/abnormal ECG.
differentiate: Seizure often has prolonged postictal confusion/stereotyped motor features; falls, intoxication and hypoglycemia may mimic syncope.
Routine head CT is low value without trauma, focal neurologic findings or another specific indication.
assessment: Obtain witness history, prodrome, exertion, position, medications, orthostatic symptoms, cardiac history, bleeding, pregnancy and family history of sudden death.
workup: ECG is core; targeted glucose/CBC/other tests answer plausible causes.
Use ambulatory rhythm monitoring, echocardiography or specialty testing according to event frequency and risk rather than ordering everything routinely.
management: Admit/escalate high-risk cardiac, hemorrhagic or other dangerous presentations.
Manage vasovagal/orthostatic causes with trigger, hydration/medication and safety strategies when serious causes are reasonably excluded.
medicationSafety: Diuretics, vasodilators, alpha blockers, rate-slowing and QT-prolonging drugs can contribute and should be reviewed.
counselling: Provide driving/work safety advice according to current CCS/provincial guidance.
followUp: Ensure rhythm/cardiology evaluation when arrhythmia remains plausible and reassess after medication changes.
examTrap: Ordering routine neuroimaging for uncomplicated syncope while ignoring an abnormal ECG or exertional event.
oneLinePearl: Syncope workup starts with story plus ECG; the dangerous clue determines disposition.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society syncope and fitness-to-drive resources

title: Anticoagulation: Match the Drug to the Indication and Reversal to the Bleed
bottomLine: Anticoagulation management requires the right indication, agent, dose, organ function, interaction profile and duration. Reversal is reserved for serious/life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedures where clinically significant anticoagulant effect matters; the antidote strategy depends on the actual drug and timing.
recognize: Warfarin effect is monitored with INR; DOACs are not routinely dose-adjusted by INR/aPTT.
Bleeding severity, last dose, renal function and the need for source control determine urgency more than a laboratory number alone.
differentiate: Warfarin, dabigatran, factor-Xa inhibitors, UFH and LMWH have different monitoring and reversal pathways.
Minor bleeding generally needs local measures/temporary dose review rather than automatic antidote use.
assessment: Confirm indication, last dose, adherence, renal/hepatic function, interacting drugs, antiplatelets, bleeding site/severity and thrombotic risk if anticoagulation is held.
workup: Use CBC/renal function and drug-relevant coagulation testing when it will change management; normal routine coagulation tests cannot reliably exclude clinically meaningful Xa-inhibitor effect.
management: Stop anticoagulant during serious bleeding, stabilize and obtain source control; use vitamin K/PCC for appropriate warfarin emergencies and drug-specific or nonspecific DOAC reversal according to current Thrombosis Canada/local availability.
Restart timing after bleeding is individualized to hemostasis and thrombosis risk.
medicationSafety: Idarucizumab is specific to dabigatran; andexanet alfa may be used for life-threatening/uncontrolled apixaban/rivaroxaban bleeding where available and appropriate but carries thrombotic risk.
Protamine reverses UFH more completely than LMWH and requires careful administration.
redFlags: Emergency surgery with significant anticoagulant effect
counselling: Teach adherence, bleeding signs, interaction/OTC review and the importance of telling clinicians the exact anticoagulant and last dose.
followUp: Reassess indication/duration, renal function, interacting drugs and whether anticoagulation should be restarted after a bleed.
examTrap: Using INR to quantify apixaban effect or giving a reversal agent for every minor bleed regardless of thrombotic risk.
oneLinePearl: Know the drug, last dose, organ function and bleed severity before choosing reversal.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada Warfarin and DOAC Management of Bleeding clinical guides, current 2026 versions

title: Pericarditis and Myocarditis: Chest Pain Beyond Coronary Ischemia
bottomLine: Pericarditis and myocarditis can mimic ACS. Use pain/ECG/inflammatory/troponin/echo context, assess ventricular function and tamponade/arrhythmia risk, and escalate myocarditis with heart failure, ventricular arrhythmia or hemodynamic compromise rather than treating all inflammatory chest pain as benign pericarditis.
recognize: Pericarditis often causes pleuritic positional pain and diffuse inflammatory ECG changes; myocarditis can cause chest pain, troponin elevation, arrhythmia or HF after infection/immune trigger.
differentiate: Regional ischemic ECG changes and coronary-pattern symptoms favor ACS; PE/aortic disease and other lethal chest-pain causes remain in the initial differential.
Tamponade converts pericardial disease into an emergency.
assessment: Assess recent infection, autoimmune disease, medications/vaccines as clinically relevant, hemodynamics, JVP, rub, HF, arrhythmia and syncope.
workup: Use ECG, troponin, inflammatory markers and echocardiography; CMR/coronary testing or specialty studies are selected when diagnosis/severity remains uncertain.
management: Treat uncomplicated pericarditis with evidence-based anti-inflammatory therapy when contraindications are addressed.
Restrict exercise and refer/admit suspected myocarditis with ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmia, syncope or instability.
medicationSafety: Avoid assuming elevated troponin in suspected myocarditis removes the need to assess ACS in an appropriate patient.
counselling: Discuss activity restriction and urgent symptoms such as syncope, worsening dyspnea or palpitations.
followUp: Reassess symptoms/inflammation and cardiac function/rhythm as indicated; myocarditis return-to-exercise is specialist-guided.
examTrap: Calling chest pain myocarditis from troponin elevation alone without excluding ACS or assessing ventricular function.
oneLinePearl: Inflammatory chest pain still needs ischemia exclusion and a stability check.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society cardiac inflammation and contemporary cardiology practice resources

title: Severe Blood Pressure: Emergency Means Acute Organ Injury
bottomLine: Hypertensive emergency is severe blood-pressure elevation with acute target-organ injury. A high number alone does not justify rapid IV normalization; the NP must look for neurologic, cardiac, aortic, renal, retinal and pregnancy-related injury and choose controlled syndrome-specific treatment when it is present.
recognize: Encephalopathy, focal deficit, pulmonary edema, ACS, aortic syndrome, AKI, retinal emergency or severe pregnancy features indicate acute organ injury.
Pain, anxiety, missed medications and measurement error can produce severe readings without emergency.
differentiate: Severe asymptomatic hypertension generally needs repeat standardized measurement, trigger/medication review and timely oral/outpatient management rather than rapid IV reduction.
assessment: Repeat BP correctly, assess mental status/focal neurology, cardiopulmonary status, volume/perfusion, pregnancy/postpartum status, stimulant/cocaine use and medication withdrawal/nonadherence.
workup: Order ECG/troponin, creatinine/electrolytes, urinalysis, imaging, fundoscopy or pregnancy testing based on suspected organ injury rather than an identical panel for everyone.
management: Emergency organ injury requires ED/hospital care with controlled IV BP reduction matched to the syndrome.
Without injury, address reversible causes and adjust oral chronic therapy with prompt follow-up; avoid precipitous normalization.
medicationSafety: Overly rapid BP reduction can cause cerebral/coronary/renal hypoperfusion.
Pregnancy/postpartum severe hypertension uses obstetric-specific thresholds and medications.
counselling: Explain why a severe reading and a hypertensive emergency are not the same diagnosis.
followUp: For outpatient management, arrange prompt reassessment and confirm medication access/adherence.
examTrap: Rapidly lowering an asymptomatic severe BP instead of first determining whether acute target-organ injury exists.
oneLinePearl: The organ injury—not the number alone—defines hypertensive emergency.

title: Cardiac Biomarkers: Injury, Congestion, and the Clinical Context
bottomLine: High-sensitivity troponin detects myocardial injury, not automatically type-1 MI; BNP/NT-proBNP support heart-failure probability but are affected by renal function, age, AF and obesity. Acute interpretation requires symptoms, ECG, serial change, hemodynamics and competing diagnoses—not a biomarker in isolation.
recognize: Dynamic troponin change with ischemic symptoms/ECG supports acute MI; stable elevation can occur with CKD, structural heart disease and chronic injury.
BNP/NT-proBNP elevation supports congestion/HF in context but is not specific.
differentiate: Type-1 MI requires acute atherothrombotic ischemia; type-2 MI/injury can occur with sepsis, tachyarrhythmia, anemia, hypoxia or shock.
CK-MB is not the preferred routine marker when contemporary troponin is available.
assessment: Assess chest pain/dyspnea, ECG, hemodynamics, renal function, rhythm, anemia, sepsis/hypoxia and known HF/CAD.
workup: Use serial high-sensitivity troponin according to the local validated ACS algorithm.
Use natriuretic peptides when they meaningfully change HF probability/assessment, not as routine screening in every dyspneic patient.
management: Treat the underlying syndrome—ACS, HF, PE, sepsis, arrhythmia or other cause—rather than the biomarker number.
Escalate dynamic ischemia, shock, pulmonary edema or malignant arrhythmia urgently.
medicationSafety: Do not start full ACS antithrombotic therapy from troponin elevation alone when a non-atherothrombotic injury is more plausible without evaluating ischemic evidence/bleeding risk.
redFlags: Rapid biomarker rise with ongoing ischemic symptoms
counselling: Explain that an elevated troponin means heart muscle injury and the cause still needs to be determined.
followUp: Ensure the diagnosed cause has definitive follow-up and risk-factor management; persistent unexplained elevation needs appropriate cardiac evaluation.
examTrap: Calling every elevated troponin a type-1 MI or diagnosing HF from BNP alone.
oneLinePearl: Troponin tells you injury happened; the clinical context tells you why.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society ACS and heart-failure biomarker resources
